findings.title: get_monitor_environment_context computes a modified config but returns the unmodified one
findings.body: The function builds a local `config` copy, replaces `schedule_type` with its human-readable display value, and then returns `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (the original, unmodified dict) in the `"config"` key of the returned context. The `config` local variable is dead code. Consequence: the monitor context sent with the issue occurrence contains the raw schedule_type value (e.g. an enum/int) instead of the display string, so downstream consumers of the occurrence event data see inconsistent/untranslated schedule type values. Either return `config` or remove the dead copy/display logic.

findings.title: get_failure_reason can raise KeyError when a single failed check-in has a status outside the known failure map
findings.body: `get_failure_reason` filters check-ins to those whose status is in `HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP` (ERROR/MISSED/TIMEOUT). If the filtered `status_counts` ends up with exactly one entry it indexes `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP` directly — fine. But if `failed_checkins` is empty or contains only statuses not in the map (e.g. a synthetic/unknown status), `status_counts` is empty, `sum(...) == 1` is False, and the function falls through to `get_text_list([])` producing an empty string, yielding the message " check-ins detected" with no counts. There is no guard for the empty case, so the evidence display can show a malformed/empty failure reason. A guard returning a sensible default (or including the raw status) is needed.

findings.title: Typo in docstring: 'humam' should be 'human'
findings.body: The docstring for `get_failure_reason` contains the typo "humam readible" (should be "human readable"). This text was carried over verbatim from the old location in mark_failed.py. Minor, but it is user/developer-facing documentation text that is wrong.

findings.title: Race between status check and MonitorIncident.get_or_create can create duplicate incidents or use a stale active_incident
findings.body: `try_incident_threshold` reads `monitor_env.status` and `monitor_env.active_incident` from the in-memory object without any locking (no `select_for_update`). Two concurrent failing check-ins for the same monitor environment can both observe `MonitorStatus.OK`, both set status to ERROR, and both call `MonitorIncident.objects.get_or_create(monitor_environment=..., resolving_checkin=None, ...)`. Depending on the DB unique constraints this can either create two open incidents for the same environment or have one request proceed with a stale `active_incident` of None, suppressing occurrence creation. The status transition and incident creation are not atomic. This logic was moved verbatim from mark_failed.py, so the race pre-exists, but the refactor is a natural place to note/fix it; at minimum the non-atomic read-modify-write of `monitor_env.status` plus `get_or_create` should be guarded (e.g. transaction + select_for_update on the MonitorEnvironment row).

findings.title: N+1 / redundant query: previous_checkins already fetched via .values() but full MonitorCheckIn rows are re-fetched by id
findings.body: When `failure_issue_threshold > 1`, `previous_checkins` is already materialized as a list of dicts containing `id`, `date_added`, and `status` via `.values(...)`. The code then issues a second query `MonitorCheckIn.objects.filter(id__in=[c["id"] for c in previous_checkins])` to fetch full model rows solely to pass them to `create_incident_occurrence`, which only uses `failed_checkin.monitor_environment` and `failed_checkin.trace_id`. This re-fetches up to `failure_issue_threshold` rows (and their related monitor_environment) that were just read. Either pass the already-fetched data through, or fetch only the needed fields (e.g. `.only("id", "trace_id", "monitor_environment_id")`) to avoid loading full rows and triggering related-object fetches per occurrence.
